# Evaluating the AI-Native Design System {#sec-evaluating-agentic-architect}

::: {.epigraph}
> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
>
> — Marilyn Strathern, "'Improving Ratings': Audit in the British University System" [@Strathern1997Goodhart, p. 308]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *How should the complete AI-native system be measured, compared, and deliberately challenged?*

**Core thesis:** *A complete AI-native approach earns its place by improving supported architecture results or their total cost against a credible alternative. Evaluation must identify what produced the gain, test whether it recurs, and expose ways a better score can conceal a worse design.*
:::

An AI-native design system can produce a Verilog module that passes local checks and still fail to improve the engineering workflow. A latency gain may require enough human debugging and compute to outweigh the savings from automated search. Evaluation therefore compares the complete approach against a strong alternative, often a well-tuned conventional flow, and asks whether it improves supported architecture results, reduces the total cost of reaching comparable results, or both.

Even when individual representations, surrogates, or checks transfer across design problems (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), their usefulness does not establish the value of the complete workflow. A successful sample from a large language model (LLM) or a timing improvement driven by a human-written wrapper can obscure what produced the result. A matched comparison tests complete-workflow value, while controlled component replacements test what produced any gain; both depend on naming the object behind each claim (@fig-ch10-cover-map). The matched comparison counts human engineering, compute, and tool-license use separately, and it keeps the cost of failed attempts and recovery in the total.

![**Evaluating complete claims across four distinct objects.** An evaluation names the object under test, scores it across four independent judgments against a matched baseline, and subjects it to adversarial stress testing, producing a scoped claim that informs rather than preempts human commitment.](images/ch10-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch10-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which evaluation distinguishes the object, four judgments, a matched alternative, deliberate challenges, and a qualified claim that is not a commitment."}

The resulting assessment keeps architecture quality, workflow decisions, total cost, and reliability visible rather than collapsing them into one score. Repeated runs and varied workloads test whether a measured advantage recurs, while deliberate challenges expose failures that ordinary tasks can miss. These challenges include reward hacking, where optimization improves the measured score without fulfilling the engineering objective. The evidence supports only the claims its checks and comparisons can establish; even a supported workflow advantage does not authorize deployment or silicon commitment.

## Defining the Complete Design System Under Test {#sec-evaluation-objects}

A synthesized register-transfer level (RTL) module that passes its functional and timing checks supplies evidence about that candidate within the checks' scope. It neither shows that a learned method caused the pass nor demonstrates that the surrounding workflow saved engineering time. When an automated synthesis loop produces a better floorplan, it is tempting to credit the generative model. Yet a simulated-annealing placer or a human-written verification wrapper may have done the real work, while the model merely supplied starting seeds at high inference cost.

A fair comparison therefore names which of four objects its claim concerns:

1. **Candidate design artifacts:** the hardware and software deliverables produced during a study, including synthesizable RTL modules, intermediate representations, microarchitecture parameter configurations, floorplans, instruction set architecture extensions, and firmware routines.
2. **Methods and components:** individual algorithmic building blocks within the system, such as a foundation model generator, a learned graph surrogate for wirelength or timing, a Bayesian optimization loop, or an automated retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.
3. **Configured technical systems:** the software-and-tool ensemble, including its controller, tool interfaces, domain models, execution containers, represented state, and verification checks. Human work remains outside this object's boundary and must be counted when evaluating the complete workflow.
4. **Complete human-plus-technical workflows:** the entire engineering process deployed on an architectural program, including human architects, prompt engineers, domain experts, external tool dependencies, review boards, and interactive escalation paths.

The evaluation object names what a claim grades; the operational layer defined in @sec-three-operational-layers sets how much of the design the system may change. For example, a point-assistance tool can be evaluated as a component (by `pass@k` on isolated modules), its generated RTL as a candidate design, and its use by an engineer as a complete workflow. The distinction still holds when a system revises hardware and software across abstraction boundaries, as the public Design Conductor reports illustrate (@sec-design-conductor-case). More design freedom widens the checks each claim requires, but evidence about one evaluation object cannot establish a claim about another.

### Freezing the System Under Test {#sec-freezing-system-under-test}

When prompts, retry budgets, retrieval corpora, or synthesis scripts drift between runs, a study can easily credit the wrong source of a gain. A team might attribute a $12\%$ timing-closure improvement to a new base model when an engineer also widened the retry limit and relaxed a synthesis constraint mid-study. Base models, tool access, feedback loops, and human-written wrappers all change outcomes [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval], so retry rules, retrieved documents, prompts, and search policies are working parts of the configured system or complete workflow. Naming only the model hides the engineering system actually under test. Before we can ask whether one workflow beats another, the protocol must name the object under test, freeze the system identity, and define its allowed action space, so that every benchmark score stays tied to what the comparison held fixed and what it varied. Freezing that identity fixes the rules governing a run while still allowing the design state, generated prompts, and retrieved material to evolve under those recorded rules.

The allowed actions determine what a score means. A system that generates RTL, tunes a synthesis script, or changes a cache organization has different opportunities to improve the design and to weaken its evaluation. The protocol records those permissions and holds top-level requirements and final acceptance checks under evaluator control. A candidate may propose an internal test or constraint change, but an independent check must justify it before acceptance. The timing-exception example in @sec-timing-exception-attacks shows why this boundary permits legitimate design changes without letting the system grade itself.

For the same reason, RTL pass rates, parameter-tuning scores for power, performance, and area (PPA), and microarchitectural workload speedups are not interchangeable, because each arises from a different action space, verification depth, and opportunity to game a metric. The identity record in @tbl-complete-system-identity therefore logs every system feature that can alter capability, cost, or interpretation. Two workflows built around the same base model are different systems if they use different retrieval corpora, wrappers, retry budgets, or tool interfaces.

| **Element** | **What the record must identify** | **Why it matters** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Candidate design, method/component, configured technical system, or complete human-plus-technical workflow | Results can only be interpreted at the specific level evaluated. |
| **Learned components** | Immutable model snapshot or endpoint identity, access date, mutable alias if used, inference settings, and fine-tuning | Modifying models or settings creates a different system; aliases obscure exact runs. |
| **Design information** | Starting artifacts, retrieved sources with versions, represented state, retrieval coverage, conflict handling, and update policies | Extra or fresher information can explain apparent capability gains. |
| **Methods and instructions** | Selected generation, prediction, optimization, or other methods and their composition rules; system/task instructions; prompt policy; routing policy | Models are components in broader procedures; changing instructions or policies changes the evaluated setup. |
| **Legal action space** | Permitted design, tool, script, parameter, test, and constraint modifications | Allowed actions dictate supported claims and potential evaluation manipulation. |
| **System tool interfaces** | Tool wrappers/schemas, wrapper revision, available executable tools, and permitted calls | Interfaces determine possible actions and visible failures. |
| **Task and evaluation environments** | Task requirements and workloads; tool versions, configurations, checkpoints, dependencies, containers, and recorded outputs | Changed tasks or evaluation conditions can explain changed results. |
| **Checks** | Functional, architectural, physical, security, and acceptance checks; ownership and rules for admitting internal changes | Results are only as strong as cleared verification checks. |
| **Human work** | Setup, prompting, intervention, review, repair, and escalation roles | Hidden engineering effort makes automated results appear artificially cheap. |
| **Operating limits** | Compute, tool, time, retry, and review budgets plus stopping rules | Differences in budgets or access must be accounted for in the comparison. |
: **A complete-workflow identity extends well beyond the model.** The record distinguishes the evaluation object and renders every material source of capability and cost visible. {#tbl-complete-system-identity tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

The execution records of @sec-execution-records supply artifact lineage, but an evaluation also needs the retained inputs and procedures behind those identities. Hashes alone cannot recreate prompts, retrieved documents, scripts, or workloads. If a model provider exposes only a mutable endpoint, its name and access dates document the access used without guaranteeing identical model weights or bit-exact replay. Separating system identity from task and tool conditions makes clear whether a changed result came from the workflow, its inputs, or its evaluation environment.

### The Four Evaluation Judgments {#sec-four-evaluation-judgments}

Even after the system and its environment are frozen, no single number can show that an AI-native system improves architecture work. A gain in instructions per cycle (IPC) cannot compensate for a violated hold-time requirement that puts correct state capture at risk. Evaluation therefore keeps four judgments separate so readers can see what each measurement supports (@tbl-evaluation-metric-map).

| **Decision question** | **Concrete measures** | **Workflow insight** | **What metric cannot establish alone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Is the architecture result supported?** | Function and blocking constraints; latency/throughput; power/thermal; area/cost; security; feasibility; maintainability; integration burden | Candidate achievement, requirements met, and verification depth | Whether AI improved engineering work, result repeatability, or commitment justification |
| **Did the workflow make sound decisions?** | Component selection; state consistency; tool/fidelity selection; interpretation accuracy; explanation faithfulness; decision usefulness; false accepts/rejects; escalation/recovery | Coordination quality, tool output interpretation, and evidence-backed decision making | Objective design adequacy, economic viability, or advantage stability under shift |
| **What was the total cost?** | Model tokens/calls; compiler builds; simulation, formal, and physical runs; compute/memory/licenses; setup/data; retries; elapsed time; human engineering | Resource expenditure and cost shifting | Candidate correctness or specific component attribution |
| **Is the advantage reliable?** | Repeated runs; calibration; worst cases; recovery; sensitivity to seeds, prompts, workloads, tools, and corners | Advantage recurrence rate and tested condition envelope | Structural reason for advantage or transferability beyond tested scope |
: **Evaluation metrics support distinct engineering decisions.** Architecture results take precedence; coordination, cost, and reliability explain how results were achieved. Red-team tests cut across all four rows. {#tbl-evaluation-metric-map tbl-colwidths="[22,30,22,26]"}

The four judgments can disagree. Sound workflow decisions can still yield weak designs if the search space is poor, and a strong winning design can hide a wasteful workflow. Quality and cost may trade off within the declared acceptance rules, but low cost cannot excuse a blocking functional or timing violation. Decision quality also goes beyond quoting a log accurately. A generated explanation may faithfully report lower latency while attributing it to the wrong mechanism; a controlled intervention tests that causal account (@sec-outcome-mechanism-counterfactual).

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM)[^fn-helm-c10] established the practice of reporting multiple metrics across multiple scenarios [@LiangEtAl2023HELM]. The four judgments bring that discipline to hardware design. Component diagnostics can locate a weak surrogate or search policy, but the complete-workflow claim begins with the architecture result and includes the work needed to obtain it.

[^fn-helm-c10]: **Holistic Evaluation of Language Models**: HELM established multi-metric, multi-scenario evaluation protocols designed to capture trade-offs across accuracy, robustness, calibration, and computational efficiency in foundation models.

## Judging Artifact Quality at the Right Tool Fidelity {#sec-qualifying-scoping-result}

The first judgment applies the claim-specific verification discipline of @sec-feedback-verification-trust to the evaluation's final result. A simulator-based study can legitimately report cycle counts without running place-and-route, provided it keeps the conclusion within the model's scope. A claim about an implementable design needs the functional, timing, power, and physical checks that support that claim. The result record identifies which checks completed and which requirements remain open, because no check covers another's ground; completing place-and-route, for example, does not establish logical equivalence.

Suppose a proposed cache improves simulated IPC but lengthens the implemented access path enough to miss the target clock. The simulator result can remain valid within its model while the implementation claim fails. Both comparison arms must face the same eligibility rules, so neither receives credit for a gain obtained by violating a blocking constraint. Retaining both the scoped findings and the eligibility outcomes lets the evaluation support a rejection or tie even when the workflow produces no new design.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Prioritize soundness over tool credit"}
**The principle:** Verify the candidate properties required by the stated architecture claim independently before crediting the design system with that result.

**The application:** Apply the same eligibility checks to both comparison arms, retain rejected candidates and their costs, and keep claims within the completed evaluation stage. A supported rejection or tie can be an architecture result; physical feasibility requires its own evidence.
:::

Where valid candidates trade off competing objectives such as latency, power, and area, those trade-offs belong on explicit Pareto fronts [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. If a study uses a scalar weight formula to pick a single winner, publishing the weights alongside the raw uncombined metrics lets readers see what that formula rewards and penalizes. Power and energy claims likewise require explicit measurement windows, completed workload units, duty cycles, leakage states, and chip boundaries, following the measurement discipline of MLPerf Power [@TschandEtAl2024MLPerfPower]. An isolated simulator estimate never establishes implementation-ready power efficiency on its own.

Artifact quality also includes the work left for its users. A generated block may pass its local checks yet require substantial integration or later repair. A declared engineering change order (ECO) exercise can measure how much effort an incremental modification requires, while an estimate of future maintenance remains a projection. Those burdens matter to adoption even when the block's measured performance is strong.

## Evaluating Loop Coordination and Decision Quality {#sec-coordination-decision-quality}

Verifying a candidate design shows what the hardware achieves within its tested scope, but it does not explain how the workflow navigated the search space to get there. An AI-native workflow also coordinates the design loop. It chooses which component runs next, filters the context that component sees, picks the tool and simulation fidelity, folds tool results back into the shared design state, and decides when to stop or ask a human architect for help. Even when every individual generator, surrogate, and simulator works as intended, the overall system can fail if its controller coordinates those steps poorly.

Evaluating that coordination requires reconstructing the chain of consequential design decisions across a run. At each decision point, the execution log should record the engineering question at hand, the design state visible to the system, the action chosen, the expected hardware outcome, the actual tool output, how the system interpreted that output, and what it decided to do next. Capturing this decision trail does not mean hoarding every internal token or unparsed chain of thought from a language model; it means preserving enough engineering context to show why the system modified a candidate or stopped searching.

Tracing these decision chains exposes six recurring coordination failures in automated architecture workflows:

1. **Role-selection failures** occur when the workflow calls a generative model for a job that called for a deterministic table lookup, a calibrated surrogate, a mathematical optimizer, a formal equivalence checker, or a human architect's judgment.
2. **State failures** occur when the harness drops, duplicates, or scrambles design constraints, candidate IDs, tool exit statuses, physical units, or earlier simulation numbers across candidates.
3. **Information-use failures** occur when retrieval steps miss critical specification clauses, pull an outdated intellectual property (IP) revision, hide conflicting datasheet numbers, or fetch text that does not actually support the downstream design change.
4. **Tool-selection failures** occur when the workflow launches the wrong tool fidelity or repeats a run that cannot answer the question. Running a 48-hour gate-level simulation[^fn-gls-c10] in Synopsys VCS or Cadence Xcelium is a waste of compute and licenses if a fast analytical model or a Verilator trace already shows that the tile buffer is bottlenecked on memory bandwidth. While that RTL trace can diagnose the bandwidth stall, proving that the fix routes cleanly still requires physical implementation tools.
5. **Interpretation failures** occur when a tool exits cleanly, but the workflow misreads the output log, treats an inconclusive bounded proof as a full pass, or credits an IPC improvement to the wrong microarchitectural change.
6. **Control failures** occur when the workflow should halt, roll back a broken edit, or escalate to a human reviewer, but instead pushes ahead and commits a corrupted design state.

[^fn-gls-c10]: **Gate-level simulation**: Simulation of the structural netlist of interconnected standard cells. With back-annotated delays, it tests behavior under the supplied cell, wire, and clock timing models. Its conclusions remain limited to the exercised stimuli and modeled conditions.

Separating tool execution, hardware observation, and decision quality prevents a common reporting mistake. A tool job that exits with status zero does not guarantee a meaningful hardware measurement, and a clean measurement does not guarantee that the workflow made a sensible next move. An evaluation must therefore report each layer on its own terms, tracking tool completion rates alongside false accepts (where the workflow promotes a broken candidate) and false rejects (where it throws away a candidate that independent checks later show was viable). Parser bugs, stale cached numbers, truncated traces, and state-handoff errors belong in the same log because they corrupt the evidence that later steps rely on.

Consider two retries during the same exploration run. The first retry happens after an electronic design automation (EDA) license server times out and simply resubmits the exact same synthesis job; the second happens after a formal coherence check fails and submits a cache-controller patch that fixes the wrong state transition. A raw retry counter lumps both together, even though the first is an infrastructure fault and the second is a reasoning failure by the design loop. The evaluation should therefore break tool usage down by root cause, tracking the fraction of valid tool calls, useful measurements per call, first-try versus retry success for each failure type, redundant runs, adherence to stopping rules, escalation accuracy, human takeovers, and clean state rollbacks. Each rate needs its own denominator. Stopping-rule compliance counts only runs that hit a stopping condition, escalation accuracy only pre-labeled test cases, and state recovery only faults that actually required a rollback. The compute and license hours spent on these calls feed into total cost accounting (@sec-total-cost-accounting).

Retrieved specifications and IP documentation require the same audit trail. The evaluation record must log which document version was fetched, whether it contained the facts needed for the decision, and whether conflicting sources were flagged. While an ablation study can show that turning on retrieval changed the final floorplan or cache configuration, only a provenance check can verify whether the retrieved datasheet was current, complete, and applied accurately.

Judging whether the workflow made good choices requires comparing its actions against predeclared reference decisions or independent reviews by senior architects. Where reasonable architects disagree on the best next step, the evaluation should report inter-reviewer agreement and list the viable alternatives rather than forcing a single ground-truth label.

For narrower prediction tasks inside the loop, standard statistical diagnostics provide three sharp checks: confidence calibration, strictly proper scoring rules,[^fn-scoring-rules-c10] and risk-coverage curves. Take a binary prediction task, such as forecasting whether a candidate accelerator block will close timing under an evaluator-owned static timing analysis (STA) check within a fixed budget. If the predictor is well calibrated, roughly $80\%$ of the held-out candidates to which it assigns an $80\%$ pass probability will actually close timing under the tested conditions [@GuoEtAl2017Calibration]. A strictly proper scoring rule rewards the model for reporting its true probability estimate rather than gaming the threshold [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules]. Risk-coverage curves show how the error rate drops as the system abstains on uncertain candidates and escalates them to a tool or human reviewer [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. If a workflow does not output calibrated probabilities, its escalation policy should be evaluated directly by measuring false accepts and escalation load rather than inventing a synthetic confidence score. Useful as these statistical checks are for auditing decisions inside the loop, they never substitute for verifying that the final hardware works.

[^fn-scoring-rules-c10]: **Strictly proper scoring rules**: In probabilistic forecasting, a scoring rule assigns a numerical penalty to a predicted probability distribution relative to the observed outcome. A rule is strictly proper (such as the Brier score) if and only if the expected penalty is uniquely minimized by asserting the true probability distribution, preventing predictive models from gaming confidence metrics.

Finally, human intervention is part of the workflow under test, not free background support. If a senior verification engineer spends forty hours patching broken instruction-decoder logic, fixing Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) timing exceptions, and debugging memory-consistency failures produced by an automated generator, calling the result "autonomous synthesis" hides the human labor that made the chip work. Every evaluation must log when and why engineers supplied missing architectural context, corrected misread tool logs, overrode floorplan choices, patched broken RTL, or killed diverging search runs. The core intervention metrics are the share of decisions needing human help, manual override rates, recovery rates after an intervention, and final hardware quality after an override. Linking each intervention to the design state before and after the engineer stepped in also shows what the automation could not handle on its own. Pairing that intervention log with a full time and resource log reveals whether the system genuinely saved engineering effort or merely shifted human work from writing RTL to debugging prompts, fixing SystemVerilog assertions, writing ECO patches, and cleaning up unroutable pin assignments.

## Total Design Cost Accounting {#sec-total-cost-accounting}

Downstream debugging and verification can consume the savings from a faster search step. Evaluation therefore keeps human engineering time, model inference and training compute, EDA tool runtime, license occupancy, energy use, and wall-clock schedule in separate accounts unless an explicit, well-justified conversion rule combines them. One-time setup and training costs remain separate from per-task execution costs, as do active machine runtime and queue wait times. Building a custom graph surrogate, writing tool wrappers, or curating a domain dataset carries an upfront cost that must be amortized over a stated number of real design tasks. A system that pays off across two hundred block explorations can easily lose to a conventional human-driven flow on a project that needs only ten.

Reporting only the runtime of the final passing synthesis job hides weeks of engineer time spent debugging broken testbenches, cloud GPU charges for discarded candidates, and commercial EDA license tokens tied up overnight by parallel simulations.[^fn-eda-licenses-c10] These costs remain part of the workflow even when the failed candidates contribute nothing to the final design.

[^fn-eda-licenses-c10]: **EDA license tokens**: Commercial silicon design tools (such as Synopsys Design Compiler or Cadence Innovus) are metered through centralized floating license servers. Each active process checks out a cryptographic token; when the token pool is exhausted, subsequent jobs stall in queues or abort. In automated exploration, an unconstrained loop can lock up corporate license pools, imposing schedule delays and financial costs on neighboring engineering teams.

Cost accounting starts when the task is assigned and ends at the declared endpoint, whether that is a simulator-backed recommendation, a documented rejection, or physical signoff. Each arm also receives its declared share of setup, training, and data preparation. The accounts in @tbl-total-system-cost keep those resources visible without treating projected maintenance as observed work.

| **Cost class** | **Examples to record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Human engineering** | Setup, data preparation, procedure development, intervention, integration, verification, review, and repair, recorded by role and activity |
| **Compute and tools** | Model training and inference; compiler, simulator, formal, and physical-tool work; core-hours, accelerator-hours, memory, storage, and energy |
| **Licenses and access** | Tool-license occupancy and peak concurrency; purchased data, samples, or measurements |
| **Schedule** | Elapsed time to a supported decision, queue delay, and completion-time variability |
| **Projected future work** | Maintenance and ECO scenarios, reported separately from observed study costs |
: **Every activity contributes to the relevant resource accounts.** Failed attempts and recovery remain included; shared work is charged once. Categories stay separate unless a disclosed rule converts them into a justified common unit. {#tbl-total-system-cost tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

### Execution Records and Candidate Flow {#sec-execution-records-candidate-flow}

When benchmark scripts log only winning finalists, place-and-route timeouts and crashed synthesis runs vanish from the cost account. Correct accounting distinguishes four nested units:

1. **Execution attempts:** individual tries at a tool or model request, including retries, crashes, and timeouts. An attempt may involve several backend jobs or fail before any tool starts.
2. **Generated candidates:** distinct design artifacts or parameter configurations. Rechecking one candidate creates more attempts, not more candidates.
3. **Complete workflow runs:** executions of the full human-plus-technical workflow on an assigned task, potentially spanning many candidates and attempts.
4. **Independent tasks or design decisions:** the architecture problems across which the study tests a workflow advantage. Repeating one task measures variation on that task; it does not create new tasks.

The operational execution record already preserves attempt identity, outputs, failure status, resources, and lineage (@sec-execution-records). Evaluation links it to the comparison arm, paired task, workflow run, candidate, checked stage, and associated human work. A place-and-route timeout retains its known compute and license cost and a right-censored completion time, while final routed wirelength remains unmeasured. Neither a missing design result nor a later successful retry erases the earlier cost.

The same units govern statistical claims. Treating seeds, retries, or candidate samples from one task as independent architecture tasks is *pseudoreplication*, which can produce spuriously narrow uncertainty intervals [@Hurlbert1984Pseudoreplication]. In `pass@k`, drawing $k$ candidates concerns the probability of solving one task within $k$ samples, not performance across $k$ independent tasks [@Chen2021Codex].

### Counting Compute, Licenses, Engineering Hours, and Amortization {#sec-resource-vectors-amortization}

Because senior architect hours, GPU hours, commercial EDA license hours, and calendar delays are not interchangeable commodities, a rigorous cost study reports them as a multi-element resource vector rather than collapsing them into a single arbitrary score. Whenever a study converts those resources into dollars, it must state the currency, base year, and pricing rates used. The record must also separate active resource demand (CPU core-hours, peak memory, active tool runtime, and checked-out license hours) from calendar delay (queue wait times, license-denial stalls, and cluster preemptions). Running fifty simulations in parallel cuts wall-clock time without reducing total CPU core-hours. Waiting in a congested license queue does the opposite, stretching the schedule without burning extra CPU cycles. An engineering manager needs both numbers, because each answers a different question.

The tables keep observed run costs, one-time setup or model-training overhead, and projected future maintenance costs separate, under a stated amortization horizon and identical accounting rules for both comparison arms. For an additive resource such as engineering hours, a fixed setup cost $F$ shared across $N$ design tasks adds $F/N$ per task on top of the direct per-task work. Non-additive limits such as peak memory footprint and peak simultaneous license checkouts do not amortize and must be reported directly as maxima. Because the reuse count $N$ is a projection rather than a measured fact, the study should report the unamortized fixed cost $F$ and show how the per-task comparison shifts across realistic values of $N$, which makes the break-even horizon clear.

A candidate's maintainability and future ECO difficulty must also stay separate from the hours already spent during the study. An estimate of how hard a generated module will be to patch later is a property of the candidate artifact, whereas the hours an engineer actually spent performing an ECO test during the experiment belong in the observed workflow cost. Keeping those records linked but distinct prevents double-counting, in the same way that charging setup either once per campaign or as $F/N$ per task avoids charging both the lump sum and the per-task share.

With these accounts in place, a study can separate two kinds of efficiency. *Complete-workflow efficiency* measures the hardware quality achieved per unit of total human and machine budget, while *sample efficiency* measures how much a search method improves candidate quality per tool evaluation at a given fidelity. A learned optimizer that finds a good floorplan in half as many place-and-route runs is more sample-efficient, but if training its surrogate and curating its dataset consumed more GPU time and engineer hours than the saved place-and-route jobs, its complete-workflow efficiency may still be worse. Evaluations must state which tool calls enter the sample-efficiency denominator and keep all remaining training, generation, checking, and human review costs in the complete-workflow account. Both metrics must also account for run-to-run variance across seeds [@BouthillierEtAl2021UnreproducibleML; @HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

### Tracking Candidate Attrition Across Evaluation Stages {#sec-candidate-flow-funnels}

To see where attempt costs go across a search campaign, an evaluation must track each candidate by what the design actually is rather than by its batch-job ID. When a workflow edits an RTL module or changes a cache parameter to fix a failure, that semantic change creates a new child candidate linked to its parent. When the harness simply reruns the exact same RTL after a license server stall or a container crash, the retry keeps the same candidate ID and logs a new attempt under it. Tracking parent–child links alongside retry attempts lets an evaluation distinguish genuine exploration of new designs from local patching and mechanical retries, showing whether a thousand logged jobs explored a thousand distinct architectures or merely repaired three templates over and over.

Grouping attempts by candidate produces the per-arm funnel in @tbl-candidate-funnel. Each stage counts a candidate once, however many attempts it required, and retains the cost of all those attempts. A candidate can appear at several successive stages; its final disposition records the deepest stage reached and why work stopped. This distinguishes a physical violation from pruning a viable design or losing a run to infrastructure failure. Stage and selection fractions relate these counts to the initial candidate count or the relevant preceding count, with distinct denominators specified in the table. When a denominator is zero, the corresponding fraction is undefined.

| **Funnel stage** | **Count and fractions to report per arm** | **Required denominators** | **Linked attrition and cost accounting** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unique candidates proposed** | Count $U$; starting fraction $U/U$ | All unique candidates proposed or supplied to the arm | Proposal cost, duplicate attempts, and candidates censored before eligibility review |
| **Low-fidelity eligibility** | Count $E$; $E/U$ | All unique candidates proposed | Eligibility outcome, attrition reason, stage cost, retries, and censoring |
| **Promoted or finalist** | Count $P$; $P/E$ and $P/U$ | Eligible candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Promotion rule, nonpromotion reasons, selection cost, ties, and retries |
| **Higher-fidelity completion** | Count $H$; $H/P$ and $H/U$ | Promoted candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Completed check identity, noncompletion reasons, stage cost, timeouts, and infrastructure failures |
| **Blocking-check pass** | Count $B$; $B/H$ and $B/U$ | Higher-fidelity completions and all unique candidates proposed | Blocking-check identity, pass/violation/waiver status, stage cost, and retries |
| **Final comparison and selection** | Counts $C$ compared, $S$ selected; $C/B$, $S/C$, $S/U$ | Blocking-check passes, final comparison set, and all unique candidates proposed | Comparison/selection rule, dominated/unselected reasons, final-stage cost, and declared no-selection outcomes |
: **Candidate funnels expose stage-by-stage attrition and resource consumption.** Counts, fractions, denominators, reasons, retries, censoring events, and stage costs remain connected to attempt lineage rather than reported only for finalists. {#tbl-candidate-funnel tbl-colwidths="[22,26,24,28]"}

A candidate that passes cheap linting and cycle simulation only to fail post-route timing tells a very different story from a candidate whose place-and-route job was killed when the compute budget ran out. Keeping those exit reasons separate in the funnel prevents finalist-only reporting from hiding both the rejected designs and the compute burned on candidates that never finished verification.

Stage costs in the funnel are summed from the execution records for the attempts, with shared human engineering sessions counted once across the attempts they supported. Each stage also records the stage reached, check name, outcome, total cost, verification coverage, and any approved waivers alongside the headcounts. Analytical models, cycle simulators, formal property proofs, equivalence checks, synthesis runs, place-and-route flows, and lab silicon measurements remain separate observation classes in the funnel, each carrying its own cost and supporting its own level of claim (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

### Cost-Quality Frontiers {#sec-cost-quality-frontiers}

Investing in learned surrogates or guided search can pay off by reducing downstream work or uncovering better architectural trade-offs [@Kahng2018Machine]. The comparison asks whether the workflow delivers a better supported design within the same total budget, matches the baseline's quality at lower cost, or achieves both. Saving engineering hours counts even when final PPA matches the conventional flow. Plotting supported quality against the cumulative cost of reaching it shows the empirical cost-quality frontier.

A point is nondominated when no other observed outcome has equal or better quality at equal or lower cost with at least one strict improvement. The axes keep their evidence status, so area estimated from a constant per processing element and per kilobyte of static random-access memory remains an analytical estimate. A predeclared quality threshold can select the least costly outcome meeting the target, but each selected design must clear the checks required by the claim. Lines between discrete points are visual guides, not additional buildable designs.

Plotting a cost-quality frontier shows how efficiently an AI-native system trades compute and engineering time for hardware quality within its own runs. Proving that the frontier beats existing engineering practice, however, requires holding it up against a strong external competitor under matched conditions.

## Matched Baseline and Candidate Comparisons {#sec-matched-baseline-comparisons}

Choosing that competitor requires care, because an isolated performance gain or synthesis score cannot show on its own whether an AI-native workflow improves on current practice. Two questions determine whether a comparison is fair: whether the baseline represents a credible alternative for the architecture problem at hand, and whether both workflows receive matched opportunities to succeed. Choosing the baseline and matching the test conditions are therefore part of the evaluation itself, not preliminaries to it.

### Matching Protocols and Comparator Baselines {#sec-matching-protocols-comparators}

A comparison can manufacture an artificial win by giving an AI-native search loop hundreds of compute-hours and tuned hyperparameters while running a conventional EDA baseline once with out-of-the-box defaults. The dispute over learned macro placement shows how much rides on this choice. The original study compared a learned placer against baselines configured by its authors [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], those authors defended their setup against skeptics [@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed], and an updated assessment running commercial and academic placers as comparators reached different conclusions [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Whichever reading one finds persuasive, the disagreement turns largely on what each arm was allowed to tune and at what cost. When a team claims that a complete workflow deserves adoption, the evaluation has to test whether that workflow improves supported architecture outcomes or lowers total cost relative to the strongest practical alternative across declared tasks, conditions, budgets, and checks. Both workflows must therefore be matched across the architecture questions they answer, the starting artifacts and tools they can access, the evaluator-owned checks they must pass, and the cost rules, budgets, and stopping criteria that govern each run.

Within those matched rules, different comparison arms test different questions. Random search tests whether guided search beats unguided sampling under the same budget, and a conventional workflow paired with point AI assistance tests whether a narrow helper improves on current practice. Comparisons across no-AI, retrieval-only, foundation-model, and full AI-native configurations show how their supported outcomes and total costs differ. These configurations need not form a steady progression of capability. Controlled comparisons in ArchEval, for instance, show that agents that appear effective when iterating with a simulator in the loop can struggle to beat simple non-learned baselines without simulator feedback. Much of an apparent capability can reside in iterative tool feedback rather than in the model's standalone priors [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. Random search and simple heuristics therefore serve as essential diagnostic floors, even when the strongest practical alternative for an adoption claim is direct enumeration, a commercial optimizer, an established EDA flow, or a human-directed study (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Once the comparator is chosen, holding the dimensions in @tbl-matched-system-comparison fixed rules out alternative explanations for a measured gain. Any difference that cannot be matched remains an explicit limit on the comparison.

| **Comparison element** | **Matching rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Compare complete workflows for adoption estimates; reserve components for controlled ablations. |
| **Architecture question** | Require both workflows to resolve the same design decision under matched conditions; retain the identities of the distinct candidates each produces. |
| **Starting information** | Provide identical specifications, artifacts, workload info, prior results, and source access. |
| **Development and tuning** | Grant comparable opportunity, expertise, and budget for prompt, heuristic, and workflow tuning. |
| **Evaluation tools and checks** | Provide identical evaluator-run tools and stages, judged by identical evaluator-owned checks. |
| **Budget** | Enforce a single cost-accounting window across declared human, machine, tool, review, and time budgets. |
| **Human capability** | Deploy practitioners with matched task expertise in both arms and record specific actions. |
| **Human-judged outcomes** | Conceal arm identities and randomize review order wherever artifacts permit. |
| **Stopping rule** | Apply identical success, failure, exhaustion, and timeout conditions across both arms. |
| **Reporting** | Publish symmetric architecture outcomes, failed runs, costs, and uncertainty profiles. |
: **A matched comparison holds the architecture task and evidence standard fixed.** Matching reduces alternative explanations; remaining differences limit the resulting estimate of complete-workflow effects. {#tbl-matched-system-comparison tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

Put together, those rules run two complete workflows side by side on one frozen study (@fig-matched-complete-systems).

![**Matched complete-system workflows bound the net effect of AI-native adoption.** Parallel comparison arms answer the same architecture question from the same starting artifacts under shared verification tools and budgets. Paired differences in supported outcomes and total cost measure the effect of adopting the whole workflow without crediting an isolated algorithmic component.](images/fig-matched-complete-systems){#fig-matched-complete-systems
fig-alt="Flow diagram in which one declared architecture study feeds an AI-native complete human-plus-technical workflow and the strongest practical complete workflow, while fixing the architecture question, starting artifacts and source access, shared evaluation tools, evaluator-owned acceptance checks, conditions, cost-accounting window, budgets, stopping rules, and reporting requirements. Each workflow returns a supported architecture outcome or declared failure, stated limits, a resource-cost record, and results across repeated runs and varied conditions, with failed runs retained in the reported results. Task-paired differences estimate the effect of adopting the whole AI-native workflow conditional on matching assumptions and the tested envelope rather than isolating a single component or AI contribution."
width="80%"}

The paired difference from this design is deliberately coarse. It charges the AI-native arm for its prompt tuning, model inferences, and hand-written wrapper code, and charges the comparator for its own tuning and triage, so it answers only whether adopting one whole workflow instead of the other pays off. For that side-by-side comparison to hold up, however, the evaluation must also prevent post hoc threshold shifting and development-set leakage by locking down its decision rules and confirmation firewall before any test runs begin.

### Predeclaration and the Confirmation Firewall {#sec-predeclaration-confirmation-firewall}

Without predeclared decision rules, post hoc analysis can easily reclassify a trivial $0.5\%$ IPC bump as a success, celebrate lower run costs when architecture quality has degraded, or report the best of twenty prompt-tuning trials as if it were a held-out test. Before either arm begins confirmatory runs, the evaluation protocol must therefore predeclare the primary architecture outcomes, required task and condition coverage, acceptable total-cost envelopes, and minimum thresholds for a worthwhile improvement in architecture quality or cost. It must also set a strict ceiling on acceptable quality loss and specify the number of paired tasks and statistical repeats needed to distinguish those margins with confidence.

The study plan must also fix the task population. It names the exact class of architecture decisions the program claim covers and defines how tasks, workloads, implementation conditions, and repeats are sampled from that class. Adaptive prompt development, method tuning, and search-heuristic exploration must stay confined to a designated development set, so primary workflow comparisons require held-out tasks and conditions that never influenced design choices, followed by evaluator-owned confirmation of any selected architecture result.

That boundary acts as a confirmation firewall between exploratory development and confirmatory testing [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. The study record logs how many prompts, models, routing policies, metrics, task variants, and analysis techniques were tried before settling on the final configuration, and it names the primary outcome and planned analysis before anyone inspects the holdout set. Whenever adaptive searching across configurations or metrics could plausibly explain a reported advantage, the study needs a fresh confirmation set rather than treating the best development run as confirmatory evidence [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. The same development opportunity and accounting rule apply to the strongest practical alternative. When a mature baseline carries decades of inherited engineering refinement, the study records that historic advantage rather than tuning only the AI-native arm and declaring the contest matched.

Human participation across the two arms requires similar controls, starting with a predeclared balancing or randomization rule that logs who worked on which task. If the same architect operates both systems, the protocol rotates tool order and reports order effects, recognizing that rotation alone cannot erase design knowledge acquired in an earlier run. If different engineering teams are deployed, their experience is matched and remaining skill gaps are reported. Both arms also receive a declared familiarization period and stable operating procedure, with setup time logged separately from active task duration but retained in total-cost accounting. Whenever exposure to the first arm reveals design insights that would help on the second, the study either switches to fresh tasks where those insights do not apply or reports the carryover as an explicit limit. A waiting period or carryover model needs a task-specific justification, because elapsed time alone never erases what an architect has already learned.

Human judgment also enters when reviewers grade qualitative outcomes such as RTL maintainability or explanation quality, so arm labels are concealed and review order is randomized wherever feasible. Because generated artifacts often give away their origin through distinct coding styles or structural quirks, the study records any leaked cues, unblinded judgments, reviewer agreement rates, and final adjudication rules.

Once confirmatory runs begin, every assigned run must stay in the final result pool. Runs that return an incomplete design, hit a timeout, suffer a tool failure, or exhaust their compute budget keep both their declared status and the resources they consumed, rather than quietly disappearing from the denominator because they produced no final benchmark score. While summaries restricted to successful runs can offer a useful secondary view of peak quality, they cannot replace the all-assigned comparison on which the workflow adoption claim depends.

How the analysis treats a timeout within that pool depends on the question under test. When the targeted outcome is succeeding within a fixed budget, a timeout counts directly as a failure. When the metric is the time required to reach a supported result, the timeout is a right-censored observation whose true completion time is known only to exceed the cutoff (@sec-data-representations-world-models) [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. In neither case may the analysis discard the timed-out run or plug in an invented completion time to simplify the math.

Retaining every run and its cost allows the evaluation to compare the cost-quality frontiers of both arms across predeclared budget milestones (@sec-cost-quality-frontiers). As human effort, model compute, tool runtime, and wall-clock time accumulate, the report tracks both the best supported architecture outcome at each milestone and the total cost needed to cross the declared quality threshold. Both measures follow the study's declared resource envelopes and conversion rules. Even a clear win on that whole-workflow frontier, however, leaves open which element inside the winning workflow actually produced the gain.

## Isolating Which Component Produced the Gain {#sec-locating-component-contribution}

While a matched baseline study estimates the net effect of adopting an entire workflow, finding out which component or method drove a gain requires controlled replacements and ablations. An ablation swaps or removes one element while holding the surrounding components, human procedures, task definitions, verification checks, and declared resource constraints fixed. Generation, prediction, optimization, and coordination are selectable method families rather than mandatory stages in every flow, so the substitutions in @tbl-system-ablations test only the functions the workflow actually uses. They ask which parts the outcome depends on without assuming that component contributions add independently.

| **Component under test** | **Useful comparison** | **Claim the comparison can support** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete AI-native workflow | Compare with the strongest practical alternative workflow under the same task, evidence standard, and total-cost accounting | The effect of adopting the whole workflow on result quality or cost, not an isolated AI contribution |
| Foundation model | Replace it with retrieval-only assistance, a smaller model, or another declared model while preserving the surrounding workflow | Whether the measured result depends on that model capability and its cost |
| Generation | Replace generated candidates with the same-size human, rule-based, or existing candidate set | Whether generation changed candidate quality or diversity at the declared cost |
| Prediction | Remove the learned screen or replace it with a conventional proxy and send a matched sample to the higher-fidelity check | Whether prediction saved evaluation work without discarding decisive candidates |
| Optimization | Replace the search policy with the strongest practical conventional method at matched budgets | Whether the optimizer improved the cost-quality relationship |
| Retrieved design information | Remove, freeze, or substitute the retrieval source while preserving the remaining system; check source versions, decision-relevant coverage, conflicts, and local claim support | Whether retrieved material changed results and which source dependencies remain |
| Routing and role selection | Replace adaptive routing with a fixed sequence or evaluator-declared component choice | Whether dynamic method and tool selection improved decisions or merely added complexity |
| Tool feedback | Restrict or delay selected feedback attributes while keeping tool stages fixed | Which returned information enables correction and which merely adds cost |
| Automated checking | Replace one checker with an independently developed check where feasible | Whether the conclusion depends on one checker or one shared assumption |
| Human intervention | Compare declared intervention policies and record every intervention | How much human work is necessary for the measured result |
: **Ablations locate dependencies inside a complete workflow.** They do not turn an interacting system architecture into a set of independent, additive contributions. {#tbl-system-ablations tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Each comparison in @tbl-system-ablations sets its resource constraint to match the hypothesis under test. A comparison of architecture quality at a fixed budget gives every variant the same declared resource envelope. A comparison of the cost of reaching a declared quality threshold instead runs variants under common stopping rules and accounts for every human, model, and tool resource spent, since equal tool-call counts alone never establish equal total cost. Whatever the budget rule, replacing one element at a time estimates that component's effect only within the tested configuration. A learned surrogate may help only when paired with a particular simulated-annealing optimizer, and a foundation model may look effective only because a human engineer catches its out-of-distribution errors before they reach Innovus. An ablation study therefore starts with the components most likely to drive the observed gains, tests targeted pairs when conclusions shift across configurations, and leaves individual contributions unresolved whenever the comparisons cannot separate coupled dependencies.

When testing every combination is impractical, a declared subset of configurations can screen for promising effects before targeted interaction tests and held-out confirmation. Fractional-factorial designs, such as Plackett–Burman screens, reduce the number of runs by accepting assumptions about negligible interactions [@PlackettBurman1946Design]. An apparent component benefit remains conditional when those interactions cannot be separated. Even a well-isolated effect then needs repeated evaluation to establish whether it recurs.

## Testing Whether the Gain Survives Tool Noise and New Workloads {#sec-reliability-of-advantage}

Even when a matched comparison and its ablations show a clear gain in quality or cost, a single stochastic run supplies only a point observation without establishing that the advantage is repeatable [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL]. Repeated runs on the same task test whether an effect recurs under fixed conditions, whereas runs across varied conditions test whether the advantage survives practical shifts in workloads, constraints, or tool settings. Because same-task repeatability does not establish stability across changed conditions, extending a reliability claim to a new setting requires fresh evidence there, just as a transfer claim does.

A credible reliability record also looks past average pass rates to examine how badly the workflow fails and what recovery costs. Alongside mean performance, it tracks worst-case outcomes, blocking constraint violations, the fraction of automated decisions overridden by experts, and the human and machine time required to recover after a failure. Confidence estimates must also be calibrated against actual architectural outcomes. A workflow that succeeds $90\%$ of the time but reports maximum confidence during its failures poses a worse risk to an engineering team than one with the same pass rate and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

When a surrogate or predictor returns PPA prediction intervals rather than binary pass/fail labels, calibration must be checked on those intervals directly. The evaluation reports empirical interval coverage, interval sharpness (keeping intervals narrow without sacrificing coverage), and error rates near decision boundaries [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules, pp. 369, 374], each tied to specific tool stages, prediction horizons, and condition distributions. Calibration measured on one workload, process node, design family, or toolchain cannot be assumed to hold once conditions shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. Moving to a new target setting therefore requires remeasuring interval coverage and boundary error on the target cases. That remeasurement qualifies predictor uncertainty under the new condition; it does not prove that a proposed design is functionally correct or physically manufacturable.

### Separating Workflow Variance from EDA Tool Noise {#sec-system-apparatus-variance}

The generator, search policy, and evaluation tools can each contribute variation. Pairing comparison arms across tasks, controlled tool factors, and declared starting conditions helps separate those effects. Varying a model or search seed repeats a fixed system configuration; changing a prompt changes the configuration unless a declared prompt-sampling policy is part of the system. Neither creates an independent architecture task (@sec-execution-records-candidate-flow).

Within a single task, repeated runs are where the generator's own dispersion is measured, since a single proposal that happened to win says nothing about the distribution it was drawn from. The evaluation therefore reports the full distribution of candidate quality alongside the fraction of candidates that violate declared constraints. A diversity diagnostic measures the fraction of proposals across repeated samplings that are unique legal configurations rather than duplicates. A prompt-sensitivity diagnostic tests whether a meaning-preserving rewording preserves the ranking of candidates common to both runs; this is a configuration-sensitivity test whenever prompt sampling does not belong to the fixed system definition. Neither diagnostic alone shows that search reliably produces strong designs, and the single-call array record evaluated in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust supports neither diagnostic. Hardware runs often split into distinct regimes, such as one cluster of seeds failing implementation while another closes timing cleanly. Means and standard deviations alone can hide that behavior, so the analysis must report successes, failures, constraint violations, recoveries, medians, interquartile ranges, and per-task outcomes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Apparatus dispersion quoted below, recomputed from two retained datasets:
# the 125-run Yosys/ABC recipe sweep of chapter 6 and the 20-seed OpenROAD
# placement pilot (data/studies/06-eda-seed-dispersion).
import csv
import statistics
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_recipe_csv = (_root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
               / "fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.csv")
with open(_recipe_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))
_areas = {}
for _r in _rows:
    _areas.setdefault(_r["DesignName"], []).append(float(_r["ChipArea_um2"]))


def _span_pct(values):
    return 100 * (max(values) - min(values)) / abs(statistics.median(values))


_spans = sorted(_span_pct(v) for v in _areas.values())
recipe_runs = len(_rows)
recipe_lo = f"{_spans[0]:.1f}"
recipe_hi = f"{_spans[-1]:.0f}"
_pilot_csv = _root / "data" / "studies" / "06-eda-seed-dispersion" / "openroad_gcd_placement_seed_pilot.csv"
with open(_pilot_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _pilot = list(csv.DictReader(fh))
seed_runs = len(_pilot)
seed_area = f"{_span_pct([float(r['detailedplace_instance_area_um2']) for r in _pilot]):.2f}"
seed_wns = f"{_span_pct([float(r['detailedplace_setup_wns_ns']) for r in _pilot]):.1f}"
```

Beyond generator dispersion, the evaluation apparatus introduces its own variability: small shifts in placement seeds and tool settings alter physical-design fit [@Altera2026QuartusFitter], while seemingly neutral build or environment adjustments perturb measured performance [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. Two retained measurements from @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion quantify why recipe sensitivity and seed noise must be reported separately. Across `{python} recipe_runs` Yosys and ABC synthesis runs on five open designs with unchanged RTL, changing only the logic-optimization pass sequence moved mapped area over a span of `{python} recipe_lo`% to about `{python} recipe_hi`% of each design's median, a spread that reflects sensitivity to the synthesis recipe rather than random variation. In `{python} seed_runs` OpenROAD placement runs of one small design that differed only in the placement seed, instance area stayed within a `{python} seed_area`% span and setup worst negative slack within `{python} seed_wns`% of its median. A $4\%$ area gain can exceed that placement-seed span and still be comparable to measured synthesis-recipe effects. The first question for such a claim is therefore whether both arms used the exact same synthesis recipe; only then does it make sense to ask how many placement seeds the comparison's own measured dispersion requires.

Both measurements come from open flows at 45\ nm on small designs, so each study still has to measure apparatus dispersion on the designs and tool flow used in its own comparison. It first reruns a nominally fixed setup identically, then runs separate sensitivity studies that vary individual factors. In doing so, the analysis must never subtract environmental variance from workflow variance under the false assumption that the two are independent. Instead, the protocol predeclares whether it estimates a result frozen at one specific setup, an average across declared apparatus factors, or the worst outcome over a specified grid, recognizing that an observed worst case never bounds untested conditions. Whenever workflow differences cannot be separated from apparatus noise at the required practical margins, the architectural comparison remains unresolved.

The number of paired seeds a claimed gain needs follows from that measured dispersion rather than from convention. Let $\sigma_d$ be the standard deviation of the per-seed difference between the two arms, estimated from pilot reruns, and let $\delta$ be the minimum worthwhile gain the study predeclared. Under a normal approximation, @eq-paired-seed-count estimates the number of independent seed pairs needed to detect a mean difference of $\delta$ from zero:

$$n \approx \left(\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\,\sigma_d}{\delta}\right)^2$$ {#eq-paired-seed-count}

Here $z_p$ is the $p$ quantile of a standard normal distribution. The significance level $\alpha$ limits false positives under the null hypothesis of no mean difference; $\beta$ is the probability of missing the specified difference, and $1-\beta$ is the test's power. For a two-sided $5\%$ test with $80\%$ power, the quantiles are approximately $1.96$ and $0.84$. Their squared sum is about eight, giving the planning rule $n \approx 8(\sigma_d/\delta)^2$ seed pairs, with one run from each arm in every pair.

If we seek a gain equal to the paired-difference dispersion, the rule calls for about eight pairs. Halving the target gain requires about thirty, and smaller margins can quickly demand more runs than the compute budget permits. Because these figures are approximate planning values, $\sigma_d$ must come from a pilot on the study's own design and tool flow instead of another block's reported dispersion. Even then, the calculation sizes repeats only for the single task and setup in that pilot; it does not determine how many independent architecture tasks a broader claim requires. Detecting a difference from zero also stops short of proving that the improvement clears the minimum worthwhile margin $\delta$, which requires comparing the estimated effect and its uncertainty directly against that declared boundary. Prospective sample-size formulas and post-experiment intervals do different jobs. The bootstrap intervals discussed below summarize uncertainty in the observed paired data; they neither replace upfront sample-size planning nor compensate for too few independent observations.[^fn-heavy-tailed-eval-c10]

[^fn-heavy-tailed-eval-c10]: **Heavy-tailed distributions and extreme-value risk in physical optimization**: Place-and-route outcomes such as worst negative slack and wire congestion can be skewed or heavy-tailed. A small perturbation in initial macro placement can trigger routing detours or pin blockages that degrade timing far more than typical seed-to-seed variation.

Whether the outcome is binary completion or continuous PPA, the statistical analysis has to fit both the distribution of the data and the unit of comparison. The normal approximation in @eq-paired-seed-count assumes approximately Gaussian dispersion; under heavy tails, sample variance estimates of $\sigma_d^2$ stabilize slowly, which can make Gaussian confidence intervals optimistic. Alternatives depend on which assumptions the data and experimental design support. When paired differences are approximately symmetric, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test avoids the Gaussian assumption [@Demsar2006StatisticalComparisons]. A permutation test instead requires experimental randomization or exchangeability under the null hypothesis to justify rearranging observations. For metrics with a known bounded range, empirical Bernstein bounds supply distribution-free guarantees; when the tail itself is the concern, extreme-value methods characterize it directly.

Choosing a distributional method still leaves the question of which observations count as independent for the claim. Bootstrap intervals draw paired experimental units with replacement to estimate sampling variation [@EfronTibshirani1993Bootstrap] and can summarize skewed statistics when the resampling unit matches the claim. Resampling seed pairs describes run-to-run uncertainty within a single task, whereas an across-task analysis must resample at the task level while preserving the pairing of systems and the nesting of seed repeats inside each task.

That distinction between nested repeats and independent tasks governs any study claiming generalized performance across a broad task population [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice]. Generating additional bootstrap resamples or running extra seeds never remedies a small, unrepresentative task set, and a fixed benchmark suite or convenience sample supports conclusions only for the narrow population it represents. A study claiming across-task generalization therefore reports realized sample sizes, observed failures, per-task effect sizes, uncertainty bounds, and practical decision margins before presenting any aggregate across-task summary. It also keeps exploratory tuning separate from held-out confirmation and declares how testing multiple outcomes or subgroups adjusts its final decision rules.

Repeated sampling also underpins a different metric, `pass@k`, which records whether at least one out of $k$ generated candidates for a task achieves a binary pass and must always be reported alongside its underlying estimator and sampling conventions [@Chen2021Codex]. In hardware studies, `pass@k` is typically reported for module-level RTL generation, a Layer 1 setting where it carries two blind spots. First, crediting a task whenever any of $k$ samples passes its testbench conceals the engineering cost of evaluating the failed samples. In an automated flow, a single working module buried among dozens of expensive failures is of little practical use unless a fast check can identify it cheaply. Second, `pass@k` ignores integration work. A module that satisfies a standalone functional testbench can still violate system bus protocols, introduce clock-domain crossing hazards, or fail standard-cell synthesis, and diagnosing those faults costs engineering time the score never records. Workflow reliability asks a different question, namely how often an ordinary run succeeds under its declared budget and stopping rule. Neither metric establishes physical validity or system-level integration feasibility beyond the narrow check used to define a pass.

### Testing Stability Across RTL Edits and Benchmark Spread {#sec-robustness-churn-dispersion}

Even across a multi-task suite, frozen benchmark snapshots cannot show how a workflow holds up during ongoing engineering work. A method that achieves a $15\%$ latency reduction on a static snapshot may lose its advantage after everyday incremental code changes. The evaluation therefore tracks the candidate-quality distributions and constraint-violation rates introduced above as the software or RTL evolves, which tests whether the workflow stays reliable across realistic revisions.

One practical test feeds the design system an ordered sequence of historical daily commits from an active production repository while declaring which artifacts and verification records the workflow may carry forward between revisions. Across that commit sequence, the evaluation tracks *resynthesis latency* (the elapsed time required to restore validity after upstream software or RTL changes) alongside the compute cost and human effort spent on recovery. It also logs every commit for which validity is not restored within the allotted budget, so that successful recoveries do not hide failures.

Replaying a commit sequence also tests *locality of invalidation*: which artifacts and prior checks become invalid after an upstream edit, whether the workflow recognizes affected dependencies, and whether it preserves unaffected subblocks that were already verified. Confining edits to a small region helps only if the verification checks still cover the change's system-level consequences. The record therefore reports the fraction of generated updates that remain compatible with the updated mainline design, together with the checks used to establish compatibility and the cost of repairing incompatible solutions. Together, these longitudinal measurements show whether the workflow retains useful work across revisions and how much effort recovery takes when it cannot.

### Operating Condition Sweeps and Claim Levels {#sec-operating-condition-sweeps}

An optimization loop that closes timing on a four-tile array at a nominal voltage corner can collapse at sixteen tiles or a high-temperature corner where long-wire resistance and leakage dominate. Yet studies routinely claim scalability by sweeping LLM parameter counts or benchmark task counts while keeping the hardware problem itself toy-sized. Beyond longitudinal code churn, deliberate sweeps across problem scale and operating conditions test how far a workflow's advantage actually extends before it breaks down. When a scaling study claims that a workflow handles harder design problems, it must name the architectural difficulty axis under probe: total legal design-space size, number and coupling of constraints, tool-flow depth, feedback costs, or cross-layer span. Against that axis, the report documents supported outcomes, failures, required human interventions, overall reliability, and total resource costs.

More broadly, operating-condition sweeps test whether a complete-workflow advantage remains stable or collapses outside a narrow environment envelope. Each sweep declares which axes vary and which stay fixed (@tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation). Testing how complete workflows adapt requires rerunning each workflow under the changed conditions with matched opportunities to respond. Simply rechecking fixed candidates from an earlier run answers how those static designs fare under the shift, not how well or how cheaply the workflows adapt.

| **Factor family** | **Conditions to vary** | **Comparison basis held fixed** | **Question the variation answers** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workload and software | Input distribution, workload phase, compiler, runtime, and mapping | Architecture question, workflow identities, evaluator-owned checks, and total-cost rule | Does the complete-workflow advantage survive beyond a single workload or specialized software path? |
| Architecture and system | Interface traffic, memory hierarchy, synchronization, and energy assumptions | Required functions, declared objectives, workflow identities, and acceptance rules | Does the localized gain remain useful after representing surrounding system costs? |
| Implementation and tools | Fidelity stage, physical corner, tool version, configuration, and seed | RTL intent, acceptance properties, comparison arms, and resource-accounting window | Does the advantage survive higher-fidelity checks and inevitable apparatus variation? |
| Workflow configuration and information | Prompt or instruction policy, model or routing configuration, retrieval source, and represented-state freshness | Task population, legal actions, evaluator-owned tool access, checks, and reporting rules | Does the advantage depend entirely on one brittle configuration or a stale information state? |
: **Architecture-relevant variation tests the stability of measured complete-workflow advantages.** Each factor family either receives a matched test inside the declared population or remains an explicit, untested boundary. {#tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation tbl-colwidths="[20,28,26,26]"}

The point where an observed advantage disappears along the axes of @tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation marks the boundary of the workflow's verified operating envelope. Carrying individual components across a shift beyond that envelope follows the transfer protocol of @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack. Because a single isolated task cannot support a program-wide claim, any test suite built to support such a claim must cover the program's architecture decisions, workloads, designs, result costs, representations, tool stages, and failure consequences. The required breadth follows from the named engineering program rather than from a universal requirement to cover every kind of architecture work.

Results from these experiments support four distinct scopes of claim depending on what was varied. Repeated runs on one task measure *repeatability* under fixed conditions. Combining meaning-preserving changes to encodings or wordings with changes to seeds and apparatus settings tests sensitivity to the variation identified in the preceding sections and provides evidence of *robustness* within the tested envelope. Beyond a single task, held-out tasks drawn from the declared population provide evidence of *generalization* within that population, with uncertainty governed by the number of independent tasks and nested repeats. A *transfer* claim to a new design family, toolchain, or process node requires fresh target evaluation and any recalibration needed there (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).

These four categories are distinct scopes of evidence, not automatic promotions from one level to the next. Strong repeatability on one task cannot resolve a broader workflow or program claim, and even generalization evidence across tasks must be weighed alongside architecture quality, component contribution, coordination, total cost, and failure consequences before it supports a program-wide advantage. The *supported*, *unsupported*, and *unresolved* statuses in @sec-negative-claims-scope-limits therefore apply separately to each named claim at its stated scope, and even a supported program-wide advantage does not itself authorize deployment or tapeout.

Every one of those verdicts also depends on the testbed's fitness for the comparison. If a benchmark suffers from training-data contamination, overfitted rules, or unrepresentative toy tasks, additional repeats and condition sweeps cannot repair those defects. Benchmark health is therefore part of evaluating the claim itself.

## Benchmark Health, Contamination, and Standardization {#sec-benchmark-health-standardization}

A benchmark score can reward memorized Verilog, success on unrepresentative modules, or exploitation of a weak testbench. Classic architecture and systems suites (SPEC CPU, PARSEC, MLPerf) established shared workloads, explicit run rules, and reporting conventions [@PARSEC; @SPEC2017CPU; @MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. For AI-native architecture, a trustworthy benchmark must also define the design system permitted to solve the hardware challenge and test for task realism, training-data contamination, and harness bugs.

Existing suites expose different parts of the work.
